title: Why 70-delta long calls are the least efficient: use 40 or 95 delta
summary: The speaker does not buy 70-delta options. For a leveraged bet he buys about 40 delta, where gamma is high, and sells or rolls when it reaches 60 to 70 delta. For stock-like exposure he goes to 95 delta, which has little extrinsic value. The 70 delta has neither high convexity nor low cost.

steps.caption: Stock at $100, one month to expiry. Both positions cost about the same dollars.
40-delta calls: high gamma between 40 and 60 delta, so gains grow fast if the stock rises.
70-delta call: more costly per contract and less convex. It moves slower than the 40s on a rally.
The difference shows the convexity the 40-delta calls add for the same money.
When a 40-delta call reaches 60 to 70 delta, the speaker sells or rolls it, or moves to a 95-delta call.

takeaways: Between 40 and 60 delta, gamma is highest: good for a leveraged bet.
95-delta calls cost little extrinsic value and leave cash as dry powder.
70 delta is the worst of both: less convexity and more cost. Roll when you get there.
caveats: The strikes and equal-dollar sizing are illustrative; the transcript shows a chart without numbers.

backtest.note: Buy one-month 40-delta calls; take profit near the 70-delta zone (about +75%) or cut at -50%.
